series.name: They Grow Up
series.tagline: The hardest days are the ones you'll miss the most.
series.concept: Each episode speaks to working parents (nuclear family, no grandparent support nearby) at a specific age milestone — from 1 week old to 14 years. Every episode validates the struggle first, then reframes it: this specific chaos is temporary, and future-you would give anything to live it one more day. Different family each episode. No recurring protagonist. The unwritten rule: your career will wait. Your kid won't.

episodes.title: No Sleep, No Help

slides.text: Your baby is 1 week old.

No sleep. No help. No clue.
No saas. No maa.
Just YouTube and WhatsApp forwards.

This tiny creature fits in your arms.
And right now, that's enough.

You don't need to be perfect.
You just need to be warm.
You already are.

Share this with a new parent running on no sleep.
They need to know — this part matters.

episodes.synopsis: First-time parents alone in a city apartment, no family support, running on no sleep. The simplest phase — and they don't know it yet.
episodes.caption: The first week is the hardest. And the smallest. And the one you'll miss the most.

episodes.title: You're Everything

slides.text: Your baby is 1 month old.

You're fighting over feeds.
Who slept less. Who does more.
'You don't understand.'

Right now, you are their entire world.
Both of you.

The fights don't mean you're failing.
They mean you both care.
That baby picked the right two people.

Send this to your partner.
You're both in the trenches.

episodes.synopsis: One month in, the couple is fighting over feeds and sleep. They don't realize they are the baby's entire universe — and that won't last.
episodes.caption: You're both exhausted. You're both trying. That's enough.

episodes.title: Back To Work

slides.text: Your baby is 3 months old.

Maternity leave is ending.
You're handing a 3-month-old to a stranger.
'Am I a bad mother?'

You're not a bad mother.
You're a mother who's doing two impossible things at once.

And tonight, when you come home,
they won't care where you were.
They'll just be glad you're back.

Know a mom going back to work soon?
Share this. She needs to hear she's not alone.

episodes.synopsis: Maternity leave ending. The guilt of leaving a 3-month-old with a stranger. These uninterrupted months won't come again.
episodes.caption: Nobody tells you how hard going back feels. You're not alone in this.

episodes.title: Were You Watching?

slides.text: Your baby is 6 months old.

First foods. First laughs. First time sitting up.
All happening between daycare drop-off and pickup.

You're not missing it.
You're working so they can have it.

And when you get home tonight,
they'll show you something new.
Because you're still the person they want to show it to.
Share this with a parent who's too tired to see what's right in front of them.

episodes.synopsis: First foods, first laughs — all happening between daycare drop-off and pickup. Parents too exhausted by evening to notice what changed today.
episodes.caption: The firsts don't wait for the weekend.

episodes.title: First Papa

slides.text: Your baby is 9 months old.

You're making dinner.
They're in the bouncer.
And then — 'pa... pa...'

You froze.
Looked at them.
They looked back and smiled.
Like they knew exactly what they did.

You called your partner.
You called your mother.
You played it on loop in your head all night.
One word. And you felt like you'd won everything.

Send this to a parent who remembers the first time.
Or one who's still waiting for it.

episodes.synopsis: Nine months old. They say something that sounds like 'papa.' Not clearly, not perfectly. But you heard it. And nothing else matters.
episodes.caption: One word. That's all it took.

episodes.title: First Steps

slides.text: Your child is 1 year old.

First steps today.
You were on a call.

The nanny tells you when you get home.
You smile. But something stings.

Tonight when you get home, they'll walk toward you too.
Be there for that one.

Send this to a parent who missed a first today.
There are more firsts coming.

episodes.synopsis: First steps happened today. You were on a call. The nanny tells you. Tonight they'll walk toward you too — be there for that one.
episodes.caption: You can't get the first one back. But there's always the next one.

episodes.title: Favourite Person

slides.text: Your child is 18 months old.

They follow you to the bathroom.
They cry when you leave the room.
You can't breathe.

They're pulling at your sleeve because
you're their favourite person in the world.

That's not a burden.
That's a privilege.
And you're the one they chose.

Share this with someone who has a toddler glued to their leg right now.
That's love, not a problem.

episodes.synopsis: They follow you everywhere. They cry when you leave. It feels suffocating. But they cling because you're their favourite person — and that's a season that ends.
episodes.caption: One day they'll stop following you. You'll wish they hadn't.

episodes.title: Because You're Safe

slides.text: Your child is 2 years old.

Tantrums everywhere.
The iPad is the only thing that works.
'Just one more episode.'

They're not giving you a hard time.
They're having a hard time.

And they chose you to show it to.
Not the daycare aunty. Not the neighbour.
You. Because you're safe.

Know a parent drowning in the terrible twos?
Send them this. They're doing better than they think.

episodes.synopsis: Tantrums everywhere. The iPad is the only babysitter. But they're not giving you a hard time — they're having one. And they chose you because you're safe.
episodes.caption: The tantrums aren't the problem. They're the proof they trust you.

episodes.title: Nobody Taught Them

slides.text: Your child is 2 and a half.

A kid at the park is crying.
Yours walks over.
Holds out their biscuit.

Nobody taught them to do that.
They just did.

You're doing better than you think.
They're proof.

Share this with a parent who doubts themselves every day.
Their kid is turning out just fine.

episodes.synopsis: Two and a half years old. At the park, they share their snack with a crying kid. Nobody taught them. They just did. And you realize — something is working.
episodes.caption: Nobody taught them. They learned it from watching you.

episodes.title: Without Looking Back

slides.text: Your child is 3 years old.

First day of playschool.
They cry. You cry in the car.
You call the school twice.
Then one day — they run in without looking back.

That sting you feel?
It means you love them enough to let them go.
That's not weakness. That's the whole job.

Share this with a parent who just survived their first school drop-off.
That sting? It means they care.

episodes.synopsis: Playschool starts. First they cry at drop-off. Then one day they run in without looking back. Relief and loss in the same breath.
episodes.caption: They're ready. You're the one who isn't.

episodes.title: A World Outside

slides.text: Your child is 4 years old.

They have friends whose names you don't know.
They sing songs you didn't teach them.
'Aarav said dinosaurs are better than cars.'

They're telling you about Aarav because
they still want you in their world.
Listen. That's all they're asking.

Send this to a parent whose kid just started school.
That window? It's open now. They should know.

episodes.synopsis: LKG. They have friends you don't know, songs you didn't teach. The window where they voluntarily share everything is open — not for long.
episodes.caption: They still want to tell you everything. Ask before they stop.

episodes.title: The Annual Day

slides.text:
Your child is 5 years old.
Annual day.

She was supposed to dance.
The music started.
She looked at the crowd.

And she just started laughing.
Couldn't stop.
Hands over her mouth, shoulders shaking.
The whole audience melted.

The performance didn't go as rehearsed.
It went better.
Because it was perfectly her.

Share this with a parent who cried at an annual day.
They'll know exactly what you mean.

episodes.synopsis: UKG annual day. She was supposed to dance. She couldn't stop laughing on stage because she was shy. The whole audience fell in love. The performance didn't go as rehearsed. It went better.
episodes.caption: She didn't nail the dance. She did something better.

episodes.title: They'll Remember If You Played

slides.text: Your child is 6 years old.

Homework. Worksheets.
'Why can't you write properly?'
Comparing with Sharma-ji's kid.

Play time is shrinking.
The kid stares out the window.

They won't remember the worksheet.
They'll remember if you played.

Share this with a parent fighting the homework battle.
They need to hear what their kid actually remembers.

episodes.synopsis: Class 1. Homework pressure. Sharma-ji comparisons. Play time shrinking. They won't remember the worksheets — they'll remember if you played.
episodes.caption: The worksheet won't matter in 10 years. The Lego will.

episodes.title: She Won The Argument

slides.text: Your child is 6 years old.

You said no.
She asked why.
You gave a reason.
She gave a better one.

Logically. Completely. In English.
You lost the argument.

You've never been prouder
of losing.

Share this with a parent whose kid
just surprised them.
It won't be the last time.

episodes.synopsis: She's 6. She argued with you — logically, completely, in English. You lost. You've never been prouder of a defeat.
episodes.caption: She's 6. She beat me in an argument. I didn't stand a chance.

episodes.title: Eating Alone

slides.text: Your child is 8 years old.

Tuition after school.
Comes home. Heats food. Eats alone.

Parents reach by 8.
'How was school?'
'Fine.'

One meal together. Phone down. TV off.
You'll be surprised what they tell you if you're actually sitting there.

Know a parent who gets home late every night?
Send them this. No judgement — just a reminder.

episodes.synopsis: Tuition, then home alone. Heats food, eats alone. Parents reach by 8. One meal together would change everything.
episodes.caption: One meal. That's all it takes.

episodes.title: Terrible Chai

slides.text: Your child is 9 years old.

Sunday morning.
You're still in bed.
They walk in with a cup of chai.
Made it themselves.

It's terrible.
Too sweet. Too milky. Slightly cold.
They're watching your face.
Waiting.

"Perfect."
You drink every drop.

Share this with a parent who's had terrible chai.
They'll smile. They'll know.

episodes.synopsis: They're 9. They made you chai for the first time. It's terrible. They're so proud. You drink every drop.
episodes.caption: Worst chai I've ever had. Best morning I can remember.

episodes.title: They Stopped Asking

slides.text: Your child is 10 years old.

They stopped asking to play.
Stopped asking for the park.
Stopped asking for anything.

You feel relieved.
'Finally, they're independent.'

They haven't outgrown you.
They're just waiting to see if you'll show up.
You still can.

Share this with a parent whose kid got quiet.
They might not have noticed yet.

episodes.synopsis: The kid stopped asking to play. Parents feel relieved. But they didn't stop wanting to — they stopped expecting you to say yes.
episodes.caption: Silence doesn't mean they're okay. It means they stopped trying.

episodes.title: Four Minutes

slides.text:
Sunday. Video call.
Dadi's face lights up.

The kid holds the phone at arm's length.
Eyes on the TV.
'How's school?' 'Fine.'
Call lasts 4 minutes.

They didn't choose to be far away.
Neither did you.
But the phone is right there.

Next Sunday, sit with your kid during the call.
Let Dadi see you both.
Four minutes can become twenty.

Send this to someone whose parents live far away.
They'll call home tonight.

episodes.synopsis: Sunday video call. Dadi's face lights up. The kid barely talks. Call lasts 4 minutes. Grandparents wonder when they became strangers to their own blood.
episodes.caption: When was the last time the call lasted more than 5 minutes?

episodes.title: The Screen

slides.text: Your child is 12 years old.

Group chats. Reels. Games.
'Dinner's ready.' 'Coming.'
They eat. Scroll. Leave.

They grew up. The world got louder.
That's not your fault.

They don't need you for entertainment anymore.
But they still need you.
They just won't say it. So say it first.

Share this with a parent whose kid lives on their phone.
They need to hear this.

episodes.synopsis: Phone is the friend now. You gave them the screen at 2 for silence. They found a whole world in there. They still need you — they just won't say it.
episodes.caption: They're not ignoring you. They just found something louder.

episodes.title: Without Being Asked

slides.text: Your child is 13 years old.

Grandparents are visiting.
You walk past the living room.
And stop.

They're sitting next to Dadi.
Phone put away.
Asking her about her childhood.

Nobody asked them to do this.
They don't know you saw.
You stand at the door a little longer.

Share this with a parent who's waiting
for a sign that it's all going to be okay.
This is the sign.

episodes.synopsis: They're 13. Grandparents are visiting. Without being asked, they sit next to Dadi, put the phone away, and ask her about her childhood. You catch it from the doorway. They don't know you saw.
episodes.caption: The closed door opens. Not for you. For Dadi. And somehow, that's even better.

episodes.title: The Closed Door

slides.text: Your child is 14 years old.

The door stays closed.
Music inside. One-word answers.

'How was school?' 'Fine.'
'Want to go out?' 'No.'

It didn't happen overnight.
It happened slowly.
And it can come back slowly too.

Knock on that door.
Not to ask if they need anything.
Just to say — I'm here.
That's enough.

Send this to a parent of a teenager.
Not advice. Just — someone gets it.

episodes.synopsis: Door closed, one-word answers. When did this happen? It didn't happen at 14 — it happened in all the years before.
episodes.caption: They didn't change overnight. You just noticed overnight.

episodes.title: Five Days

slides.text: Diwali. Dadi's been waiting for months.

The kid she remembers used to climb into her lap.
This one is taller than her.

She brought their favourite sweets.
'Thanks, Dadi.'
Back to the phone.

Dada tries to teach them chess.
'I have homework.'

5 days isn't much.
But Dadi doesn't need much.
She just needs to be in the room.

Share this with your siblings.
Then call your parents. Together.

episodes.synopsis: Annual Diwali visit. Dadi's been waiting months. The kid she knew is gone. 5 days a year can't bridge 360 days of absence.
episodes.caption: They came for 5 days. They left feeling like strangers.
